source.title: The Randomness of Input Data Spaces is an A Priori Predictor for Generalization
source.authors: Martin Briesch; D. Sobania; Franz Rothlauf

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no material garbling or cutoff affecting the reported experiments.
record.tranche_reason: The study randomizes labels and inputs, trains neural networks to 100% training accuracy, and reports generalization error, directly applying the core intervention and measures relevant to the claims.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for randomized labels and four input-randomization variants. It also discusses Arpit et al.'s easy and hard examples, but does not measure the training-time order in which real and random labels are learned. Values in Figs. 2–5 are figure-only; the paper does not give recoverable numeric values for individual plotted conditions in the text.
record.test_reason: The study independently randomizes labels and inputs, reports training to 100% accuracy with Adam, and measures test error. Its predictor of generalization is the main contribution, but its own fitting results bear directly on V1, V3 and V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that randomness of label sequences generated by walks through the input-data landscape can serve as an a priori indicator of expected generalization error. Their evidence is correlational and limited to binary classification; natural-data results also depend on the approximated manifold and neighborhood.
record.recipe_differences: Uses label randomization as in the cited approach and measures train fit and generalization, but focuses on input-space randomness as a predictor, uses synthetic and image datasets, and trains specified MLP/CNN architectures with Adam.
record.method_sensitivity: Input-randomization effects differ between MNIST and CIFAR10; the text notes a lower PermutGlobal effect for MNIST and differences for PermutInd associated with dataset statistics.

fits_no_version.finding: Maurer-test statistics from label-landscape random walks correlate strongly with generalization error across the studied datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label-landscape randomness predicts generalization error in the tested binary classification settings.

record.problems: Generalization values for individual conditions are shown only in figures. Results are averaged over 30 runs; the text does not report uncertainty intervals or per-condition numerical values. Experiments are limited to binary classification.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The easy-versus-hard cats and dogs comparison in Fig. 5 concerns sample selection and generalization, not any listed claim version, and is not separately extracted.

untested.parts: The supplied text does not identify the exact fully randomized endpoint or its test error. Architecture is specified by dataset, but unchanged optimizer hyperparameters across corruption conditions are not documented; the general assertion about unchanged hyperparameters cites prior work.
No training-time ratios or convergence-speed comparisons across corruption fractions.

Exact monotonicity and the chance endpoint cannot be checked from the supplied figure text. Because test labels are also corrupted, increasing test error does not independently establish how well the remaining clean signal is learned.
No comparisons involving weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, or their removal.
No trajectories comparing learning of real labels with memorization of noisy labels. Easy-versus-hard sample selection after one epoch does not test that ordering.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 limits_scope verdict confuses incomplete evidence with an observed failure. No stated result establishes an absent or reversed effect. The supplied text contains figure captions but no readable plotted values, so precise endpoint errors cannot be recovered.

versions.untested_parts: The text does not provide per-condition numeric training or test errors; it states that models were trained to 100% training accuracy and shows generalization error in figures.
Training time comparisons and convergence speed as corruption increases are not reported.
The paper tests four input-randomization variants, but does not separately report a condition explicitly named shuffled pixels.
The paper describes declining generalization with stronger label randomization, but does not textually establish a steady increase toward chance at every corruption level.
Weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, and their removal are not studied.
The paper does not track learning over training to compare when real versus random labels are learned.
